title: Docker and Docker Compose
theme: Package ShopNotes in safe, small images, run the full stack with Compose, scan the images and push them to a registry.
jobStory: In this sprint you put the ShopNotes API and web page into Docker images. You write multi-stage Dockerfiles, add health checks and run the full stack with one docker compose command. You push versioned images to GitHub Container Registry and scan them with Trivy, like a security team asks at real companies. You also write a runbook so the team can use Docker without asking you.
outcomes: I wrote multi-stage Dockerfiles that run as a non-root user with a health check and a .dockerignore.
I ran Postgres, the API and Nginx with Docker Compose, with health-based start order and a saved volume.
I pushed versioned images to GitHub Container Registry.
I scanned images, Dockerfiles and the repo with Trivy and fixed the high findings.
I wrote a Docker runbook with real errors and fixes.

tickets.title: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile and .dockerignore for the API
tickets.goal: The ShopNotes API runs from a small Docker image that is built in two stages, runs as a normal user and has a health check.
tickets.context: Hi, every developer has a different laptop and "it works on my machine" costs us time. Please put the API in a Docker image. Keep the image small, do not run as root, and do not copy secrets or the .venv folder into it.
steps: Install Docker Engine by following the official guide for Ubuntu (link in resources). On Windows you can use Docker Desktop with the WSL2 backend instead. Then let your user run Docker: `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, log out and in again, and test with `docker run --rm hello-world`.
Check the versions: `docker version` and `docker compose version`. Compose v2 is the `docker compose` plugin (with a space). The old `docker-compose` (with a dash) is not used any more.
Create `api/.dockerignore` with these lines: `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.env`, `.git`, `tests/`, `*.md`. Files in this list are not sent to the Docker build.

Create `api/Dockerfile`. Stage 1 (build): `FROM python:3.12-slim AS build`, `RUN python -m venv /opt/venv`, `ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"`, `COPY requirements.txt .`, `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`.

Stage 2 (runtime) in the same file: `FROM python:3.12-slim`, `RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 app`, `COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv`, `ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `WORKDIR /app`, `COPY app.py .`, `USER app`, `EXPOSE 5000`.

Add a health check and the start command at the end: `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=2)"` and `CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "--workers", "2", "--access-logfile", "-", "app:app"]`. Inside a container the app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
Stop the systemd service from sprint 1 so port 5000 is free: `sudo systemctl stop shopnotes`.
Build the image: `docker build -t shopnotes-api:dev ./api`. See the size: `docker images shopnotes-api`.

Run it with your laptop database. On Linux use the host network: `docker run --rm -d --name api --network host -e DATABASE_URL=postgresql://shopnotes:shopnotes@localhost:5432/shopnotes shopnotes-api:dev`. Then `curl http://localhost:5000/health`. (With Docker Desktop, use `-p 5000:5000` and `host.docker.internal` instead of `localhost` in the URL.)
After 30 seconds check the health status: `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' api`. It must be `healthy`.
Check the user and the files in the image: `docker exec api id` (uid=10001) and `docker exec api ls -la /app` (only `app.py`, no `.venv`, no `.env`). Stop it: `docker stop api`.

For comparison, write a one-stage file `api/Dockerfile.single`: `FROM python:3.12`, `WORKDIR /app`, `COPY . .`, `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`, `CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "app:app"]`. Build it with `docker build -f api/Dockerfile.single -t shopnotes-api:single ./api` and compare with `docker images shopnotes-api`. Write both sizes in your PR, then delete `Dockerfile.single`.
Commit `api/Dockerfile` and `api/.dockerignore` through a PR.
acceptance: `docker build -t shopnotes-api:dev ./api` works without errors.
`docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' api` shows `healthy`.
`docker exec api id` shows uid 10001, not root.
`/app` in the container has no `.venv`, `.env` or `.git`.
The PR shows the image size of the single-stage and the multi-stage build.
evidence: Output of `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' api` and `docker exec api id`
Link to the merged PR with the Dockerfile
hints: `permission denied ... docker.sock` means your user is not in the docker group yet. Log out and log in again after `usermod`.
Put `COPY requirements.txt` before `COPY app.py`. Then Docker reuses the cached pip layer when only the code changes.
If the container stops at once, read why with `docker logs api`.

explain.en: In this task I put the ShopNotes API in a Docker image. I wrote a multi-stage Dockerfile: the first stage installs the Python packages into a virtual environment, and the second stage copies only that environment and app.py. The container runs as a normal user with uid 10001, not root. I added a HEALTHCHECK that calls /health, and a .dockerignore so .venv, .git and .env never go into the image. I compared the size with a single-stage build and wrote the result in the pull request.

vocabulary.en: a packed file system plus settings, used to start containers
a running copy of an image, isolated from other programs
a Dockerfile with more than one FROM, where the last stage keeps only what is needed
one saved step of an image; Docker reuses layers that did not change
a list of files that Docker must not send into the build

interview.q: Why did you use a multi-stage build?
interview.a: The first stage has pip and all build files. The final stage copies only the finished virtual environment and the code. So the final image is smaller and has fewer tools an attacker could use. Small images also download faster on servers.

interview.q: Why does the container not run as root?
interview.a: If someone breaks into the app, root inside the container gives them much more power. With a normal user they can do less damage. So I create a user with useradd and switch to it with USER before the CMD.

Docker runs the health command every 30 seconds inside the container. If it fails 3 times, the container is marked unhealthy. Docker Compose can wait for healthy before it starts other services, and I can see the status in docker ps.

tickets.title: Run the full ShopNotes stack with Docker Compose
tickets.goal: One `docker compose up` starts Postgres, the API and the web front end, in the right order, with health checks and a saved database volume.
tickets.context: Hi, new people still need one hour to install Postgres and Nginx. Please make the whole app start with one command. Use Docker Compose for the database, the API and the web page. The API must wait until the database is really ready, and the data must survive a restart.
steps: Create `web/nginx.conf`: `server { listen 80; root /usr/share/nginx/html; location / { try_files $uri /index.html; } location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api:5000/; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; } }`. Here `api` is the name of the Compose service, Docker DNS finds it.

Create `web/Dockerfile`: `FROM nginx:stable-alpine`, `COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`, `COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html`, `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ >/dev/null || exit 1`.

Create a file `.env` in the repo root with `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-local`. It is already in `.gitignore`. Also create `.env.example` with `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=` (empty) and commit that one, so people know what to set.

Create `compose.yaml` in the repo root. Service `db`: `image: postgres:16`, `environment:` `POSTGRES_USER: shopnotes`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set it in .env}`, `POSTGRES_DB: shopnotes`; `volumes:` `- dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data` and `- ./db/schema.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-schema.sql:ro`.
Give `db` a health check: `healthcheck:` `test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shopnotes -d shopnotes"]`, `interval: 5s`, `timeout: 3s`, `retries: 10`.

Service `api`: `build: ./api`, `image: shopnotes-api:dev`, `environment:` `DATABASE_URL: postgresql://shopnotes:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/shopnotes`, `depends_on:` `db:` `condition: service_healthy`, `ports: ["127.0.0.1:5000:5000"]`, `restart: unless-stopped`.

Service `web`: `build: ./web`, `image: shopnotes-web:dev`, `ports: ["8080:80"]`, `depends_on:` `api:` `condition: service_healthy`, `restart: unless-stopped`. At the end of the file add the named volume: `volumes:` `dbdata: {}`.
Check the file: `docker compose config`. It prints the final config or a clear error.
Stop the old laptop services so the ports are free: `sudo systemctl stop shopnotes nginx`. Then start the stack: `docker compose up -d --build`.
Watch the start order: `docker compose ps`. `db` becomes healthy first, then `api`, then `web`. Read logs with `docker compose logs -f api` (Ctrl+C to stop reading).

Test it: `curl http://localhost:8080/api/health`, `curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"text":"from compose"}' http://localhost:8080/api/notes`, and open http://localhost:8080 in the browser.
Look inside the database: `docker compose exec db psql -U shopnotes -d shopnotes -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM notes;'`.

Test that data survives: `docker compose down` (containers removed, volume kept), `docker compose up -d`, the notes are still there. Then see what `-v` does: `docker compose down -v` removes the volume and the data. Start again and the table is created fresh by `01-schema.sql`.
Test the health wait: `docker compose stop db`, call `/api/health` (503), `docker compose start db`, call it again (200).
Add a `Run with Docker` part to the README (`cp .env.example .env`, set a password, `docker compose up -d --build`, open http://localhost:8080). Commit through a PR.
acceptance: `docker compose up -d --build` starts 3 services and `docker compose ps` shows all of them `healthy`.
http://localhost:8080 shows the page and you can add notes in the browser.
Notes are still there after `docker compose down` and `docker compose up -d`.
`/api/health` gives 503 while `db` is stopped and 200 after it starts again.
No real password is in Git: `.env` is ignored and `.env.example` is committed.
evidence: Output of the curl tests through port 8080
hints: Files in `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/` run only when the data volume is empty. If you change `schema.sql`, run `docker compose down -v` to start fresh.
If `web` exits with `host not found in upstream "api"`, the API was not ready. Check that `depends_on` uses `condition: service_healthy`.
Use `docker compose logs <service>` before you change anything.

explain.en: In this task I made the whole app start with one command, docker compose up. The compose file has three services: Postgres, the API and an Nginx web container that sends /api/ to the API. I used health checks with depends_on condition service_healthy, so the API waits until the database is really ready. The database data lives in a named volume, so it survives docker compose down. The password comes from a .env file that is not in Git. I tested the start order, the data after a restart, and the 503 when the database is stopped.

vocabulary.en: a tool that starts many containers from one YAML file
one part of a compose file, like db, api or web
storage that Docker keeps even when the container is removed
a compose setting that controls which service starts first
Docker gives each service a name that other containers can use as a host name

interview.q: How do you make sure the API starts only after the database is ready?
interview.a: A running Postgres container is not always ready to accept connections. So I gave the db service a health check with pg_isready. The api service has depends_on with condition service_healthy, so Compose waits until the health check passes.

interview.q: Why do you use a named volume for Postgres?
interview.a: Containers are thrown away and created again often. Without a volume, all data would be lost on docker compose down. The named volume dbdata keeps the data outside the container. Only docker compose down -v deletes it.

interview.q: How do you keep passwords out of the compose file?
interview.a: I write ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} in the compose file and keep the real value in a .env file. The .env file is in .gitignore. I commit a .env.example with empty values so new people know what to fill.

tickets.title: Push the ShopNotes images to GitHub Container Registry
tickets.goal: Version 0.1.0 of the API and web images is in GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io) and anyone on the team can pull it.
tickets.context: Hi, our servers cannot build images from your laptop. Please push the images to GitHub Container Registry with a real version tag. Link them to our repo and make them public, so servers can pull them without a password.
steps: Create a token for the registry: on GitHub go to Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens > Tokens (classic) > Generate new token (classic). Give it only the scope `write:packages` (it also adds `read:packages`) and an expiry of 30 days.

Log in without saving the token in your shell history: `read -s CR_PAT` (paste the token, press Enter), then `echo "$CR_PAT" | docker login ghcr.io -u <your-github-user> --password-stdin`. You must see `Login Succeeded`.
Link the images to the repo. Add this line to `api/Dockerfile` and `web/Dockerfile` (in the last stage): `LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/<your-github-user>/shopnotes"`.

Build with two tags each. Registry names must be lowercase: `docker build -t ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:0.1.0 -t ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:latest ./api` and the same for web: `docker build -t ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-web:0.1.0 -t ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-web:latest ./web`.
Push all tags: `docker push --all-tags ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api` and `docker push --all-tags ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-web`.
On GitHub open your profile > Packages. Open each package > Package settings > Change visibility > Public. Check that the package page shows your shopnotes repo.

Test a pull like a server would: `docker logout ghcr.io`, `docker rmi ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:0.1.0`, `docker pull ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:0.1.0`. It must work without login.

Let Compose use the registry images too: in `compose.yaml` change the image names to `image: ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:${TAG:-dev}` and `image: ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-web:${TAG:-dev}` (keep `build:`). Now `TAG=0.1.0 docker compose pull` and `TAG=0.1.0 docker compose up -d` run the released version without building.
Remember the rule: `latest` is only a moving label. Servers always deploy a fixed version like `0.1.0`.
Commit the Dockerfile and compose changes through a PR. Never commit the token.
acceptance: Both packages `shopnotes-api` and `shopnotes-web` exist on ghcr.io with tags `0.1.0` and `latest`.
Both packages are public and linked to the shopnotes repo.
`docker pull ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/shopnotes-api:0.1.0` works after `docker logout ghcr.io`.
`TAG=0.1.0 docker compose up -d` runs the stack from the registry images.
evidence: Links to both package pages on GitHub
Output of the `docker pull` after logout
hints: `denied: permission_denied` usually means the token has no `write:packages` scope or the name has capital letters.
If you lose the token, delete it on GitHub and create a new one. Never paste a token in chat or in a file in the repo.
GitHub Packages accepts only classic personal access tokens for `docker login`. A fine-grained token will not work here.

explain.en: In this task I pushed our API and web images to GitHub Container Registry. I made a classic token with only the write:packages scope and logged in with --password-stdin, so the token is not in my shell history. I added the org.opencontainers.image.source label so each package is linked to our repo. I pushed a fixed version 0.1.0 and latest, made the packages public, and tested a pull after logout. Compose can now run a released version with TAG=0.1.0 without building anything.

vocabulary.en: a server that stores images so others can pull them
a name for one version of an image, like 0.1.0
a long secret string that works like a password for one job
the list of things a token is allowed to do
to download an image from a registry

interview.q: Why do you not deploy the latest tag?
interview.a: latest is just a label that moves to the newest push. If I deploy latest, I do not know which code is running, and a rollback is hard. A fixed tag like 0.1.0 always points to the same image, so deploys are repeatable.

interview.q: How did you log in to the registry safely?
interview.a: I used a token with only the write:packages scope and a short expiry. I read it with read -s and passed it with --password-stdin, so it is not in the shell history or in the process list. I never put the token in Git.

interview.q: What is the image source label for?
interview.a: The label org.opencontainers.image.source tells GitHub which repo the image comes from. GitHub then shows the package on the repo page and can use the repo permissions. It also helps people find the code for an image.

tickets.title: Scan the images with Trivy and fix high findings
tickets.goal: The API and web images have no fixable HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerabilities, and the Dockerfile and repo pass a Trivy config and secret scan.
tickets.context: Hi, a customer asked if our images are safe. Please scan them with Trivy, fix what can be fixed and write down what is left with a reason. Also check the repo for secrets and the Dockerfiles for bad settings.
steps: Install Trivy with the official install script: `curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin`. The official install page shows how to pin a version and other ways (apt, Docker). Check: `trivy --version`.
Scan the API image: `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL shopnotes-api:dev`. Read the table: Library, Vulnerability (CVE id), Severity, Installed Version, Fixed Version.

Scan again and show only problems that have a fix: `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed shopnotes-api:dev`. Write the number of findings for both scans in a file `docs/security/trivy-notes.md`.
Fix OS findings by rebuilding on the newest base image: `docker build --pull -t shopnotes-api:dev ./api`. `--pull` downloads the newest `python:3.12-slim` with security patches.

Fix Python findings: for each Python library in the list, raise the version in `api/requirements.txt` to at least the Fixed Version. Rebuild, run the app with Compose and test `/api/health` again. A fix that breaks the app is not a fix.
Scan the web image too: `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed shopnotes-web:dev`, and fix it the same way (`docker build --pull ...`).
Scan the Dockerfiles for bad settings: `trivy config api/` and `trivy config web/`. Read each finding (for example a missing USER or HEALTHCHECK) and fix it or explain it.
Scan the whole repo for secrets and vulnerable packages: `trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret .`. If it finds a real secret, remove it, change (rotate) the secret, and tell your lead.

If a finding has no fix and you must accept it for now, add the CVE id to a file `.trivyignore` in the repo root, with a comment line above it: why it is OK, who decided, and a review date (for example `# no fix yet in Debian, not reachable from our code, review 2026-12-01`).
Make Trivy a gate: `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed shopnotes-api:dev; echo $?`. Exit code 1 means the build must stop. In sprint 3 the CI pipeline will use this.
Write the before and after numbers in `docs/security/trivy-notes.md` and commit everything through a PR.
acceptance: `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed` shows 0 findings for both images, or every finding left is in `.trivyignore` with a reason and a date.
`trivy config api/` and `trivy config web/` have no HIGH findings left without a written reason.
`trivy fs --scanners secret .` finds no secrets.
`docs/security/trivy-notes.md` has the before and after numbers.
The app still works after the updates (`/api/health` is 200).
evidence: Trivy output before and after the fixes (paste the summary lines)
Output of the gate command with `echo $?`
hints: The first scan downloads the vulnerability database and can take a minute. Later scans are fast.
Many OS findings go away just with `docker build --pull`. Try that first.
Do not ignore a CVE only to make the scan green. Every ignore needs a reason and a review date.

explain.en: In this task I scanned our Docker images with Trivy. First I counted the HIGH and CRITICAL findings, then I used --ignore-unfixed to see the ones we can really fix. I rebuilt with --pull to get the newest base image patches and raised Python library versions in requirements.txt. I also ran trivy config on the Dockerfiles and trivy fs to look for secrets in the repo. For one finding without a fix I wrote a .trivyignore entry with a reason and a review date. In the end both images had no fixable high findings and the app still worked.

vocabulary.en: a known weakness in software that an attacker can use
a public id number for one known vulnerability, like CVE-2024-1234
how dangerous a finding is: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL
the image in the FROM line that your image starts from
a check that stops the pipeline when it finds a serious problem

interview.q: How do you fix vulnerabilities in a Docker image?
interview.a: First I rebuild with --pull, because many fixes come with a newer base image. Then I update the app libraries to the fixed version and test the app. If there is no fix yet, I document it with a reason and a review date instead of hiding it.

interview.q: What does --ignore-unfixed do and why use it?
interview.a: It hides findings that have no fixed version yet. I use it for the pipeline gate, because the team cannot fix those today and a red build for them helps nobody. But I still look at the full list and watch for fixes.

interview.q: What else can Trivy scan besides images?
interview.a: trivy fs scans a folder for vulnerable packages and leaked secrets. trivy config checks Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML and Terraform for bad settings. I used both on our repo, not only the image scan.

tickets.title: Write the Docker runbook for the team
tickets.goal: The team has one page that explains how to build, run, debug, release and clean up ShopNotes with Docker.
tickets.context: Hi, people keep asking me the same Docker questions on chat. Please write one runbook with the commands we really use: start, logs, shell, release, scan and clean up, plus the common errors you saw this sprint.
steps: Create `docs/docker.md` with these headings: Overview, Start and stop, Logs and shell, Environment variables, Ports and volumes, Release a new version, Security scan, Clean up, Troubleshooting.
Overview: a text diagram `browser -> web (nginx :8080) -> api (gunicorn :5000) -> db (postgres :5432, volume dbdata)`.
Start and stop: `docker compose up -d --build`, `docker compose ps`, `docker compose stop`, `docker compose down`, and a warning in bold that `docker compose down -v` deletes the database data.
Logs and shell: `docker compose logs -f api`, `docker compose logs --tail 50 web`, `docker compose exec api sh`, `docker compose exec db psql -U shopnotes -d shopnotes`.
Environment variables: a table with Name, Used by, Example, Secret (yes/no). Include `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `DATABASE_URL` and `TAG`.
Release a new version: the build, tag and push commands from OPS-203 with `<version>` in place of 0.1.0, and how to pick the next version number.
Security scan: the Trivy commands from OPS-204 and where `.trivyignore` lives.
Clean up: `docker system df` to see used space, `docker image prune` for dangling images, `docker builder prune` for old build cache. Explain what each one deletes.

Troubleshooting: at least 4 errors you saw, with the fix. Ideas: port already in use (`sudo ss -ltnp | grep 8080`), permission denied on docker.sock, db unhealthy because of a wrong password in the volume (needs `down -v`), web says host not found in upstream.
Add a link to `docs/docker.md` in the README and merge through a PR.
acceptance: `docs/docker.md` has all 9 headings with real, tested commands.
The env table lists every variable and marks secrets.
Troubleshooting has at least 4 real errors with fixes.
The README links to the new page.
hints: Copy commands from your terminal history (`history | grep docker`), so they are real and tested.
Write the error message exactly as Docker prints it. People search for it.
Mark dangerous commands (like `down -v` or `system prune -a`) clearly.

explain.en: In this task I wrote the Docker runbook for the team. It explains how to start and stop the stack, read logs, open a shell, release a new image version and scan it with Trivy. I added a table of all environment variables and marked which ones are secrets. I also wrote the clean-up commands with a clear warning about what they delete, and four real errors from this sprint with their fixes. Now people can find answers on one page instead of asking on chat.

vocabulary.en: an old image layer with no tag, left after rebuilds
saved build steps that make the next build faster
two programs try to use the same port on one machine
finding the cause of a problem step by step

interview.q: How do you debug a container that keeps restarting?
interview.a: First I run docker compose ps to see the state and the exit code. Then I read docker compose logs for that service, because the error is usually there. If it starts for a moment, I open a shell with docker compose exec and check the files and environment variables.

interview.q: How do you free disk space used by Docker safely?
interview.a: I start with docker system df to see what uses space. Then I remove dangling images with docker image prune and old build cache with docker builder prune. I am careful with volumes, because docker volume prune can delete database data.

interview.q: Why write a runbook if the commands are in your head?
interview.a: I am not always online, and people forget. A runbook lets anyone in the team fix a common problem quickly and the same way. It also helps a new person learn the system faster.
